opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I value most is that it keeps us honest. It's easy, building models in a vacuum, to optimize for benchmarks that look great on a leaderboard but don't map onto what a medicinal chemist or a structural biologist actually needs on a Tuesday afternoon. When you work closely with pharma teams, you get immediate, sometimes humbling feedback: does this design actually bind? Is it developable? Can we make it? Does it get us somewhere faster than the approaches we already trust?

The second thing is the problems themselves. The targets pharma partners bring are the hard ones: targets that have resisted traditional approaches for years, sometimes decades. That's where the potential of these models really gets tested, and it's where you learn the most about where the models break.

Third, there's a complementarity I find exciting. We bring the modeling and the ability to explore design space computationally at a scale that wasn't possible before. They bring deep biological intuition, wet-lab capacity, clinical know-how, and the institutional knowledge of what it takes to turn a molecule into a medicine. Neither side gets to the finish line alone. A model can propose a beautiful binder, but getting it into patients is a very long road, and partners who have walked that road many times are invaluable.

And finally, I think it's the right way to have impact. Our goal isn't to publish a cool paper. It's to help get better drugs to patients sooner. Partnerships are how what we build actually leaves the computer and enters the real world.

r002.rationale: It mentions practical feedback from close work with pharma teams, but does not say partners use Chai’s models in actual campaigns or that this use grounds the feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what I value most is that the partnership model forces us to be accountable to reality. It's really easy in AI for drug discovery to build a model, publish a benchmark, get a nice number on some retrospective dataset, and convince yourself you've done something useful. When you're working with a pharma partner, none of that matters. What matters is: did the molecules we designed actually bind? Did they have the properties the medicinal chemists needed? Did we save them months on a program that was stuck? You get a very fast, very unforgiving feedback signal, and that signal has shaped Chai-2 more than almost anything else.

The second thing is access to problems we'd never see on our own. The really hard, really valuable targets in pharma are the ones nobody's been able to crack with conventional approaches, and those don't show up in public datasets. Partners bring us those targets, and in exchange we bring a platform that can do things like zero-shot antibody design against epitopes they've been chasing for years. That's a genuinely complementary trade. They have the biology, the assays, the clinical know-how, and the patience to take something through the clinic. We have the models. Neither side is pretending to be the other.

And the third piece, which I think people underrate, is the trust that comes from working on real programs together over time. Early on there's a lot of skepticism, understandably. Pharma has heard the AI pitch many times. But once you've been through a couple cycles where the computational predictions actually hold up in the wet lab, the conversation changes. It stops being "prove to us this works" and becomes "what else can we point this at?" That shift, from vendor to collaborator, is where the model really starts paying off for both sides. It also keeps us honest about staying a platform company rather than trying to become a pharma company ourselves, which is a trap a lot of groups in this space fall into.

We bring the AI and computational capabilities, and pharmaceutical partners bring deep knowledge of the biology, the clinical need, and what it takes to develop a medicine. The most useful partnership is a close feedback loop: we design something, test it together, understand what worked and what didn’t, and use that to guide the next round. That keeps the work grounded in problems that matter to patients.

Pharmaceutical partners bring a deep understanding of the biology and what a successful therapeutic needs to look like. We bring our approach to molecular design. The useful part is the feedback between those perspectives: making sure we’re asking the right questions, learning from experimental results, and using that learning to guide the next design.
